question: Awnik repeatedly plays a game that has a probability of winning of \(\dfrac{1}{3}.\) The outcomes of the games are independent. What is the expected value of the number of games he will play until he has both won and lost at least once?
solution:
After the first game, Awnik needs only the opposite outcome. We can therefore find the expected additional wait separately for a first-game win and a first-game loss.

First, suppose a desired outcome has probability \(p>0\) on each independent trial. Let \(g_m\) be the expected wait when we stop at that outcome or after \(m\) trials, whichever comes first. Then \(g_0=0\), and splitting according to the first trial gives
\[
g_m=1+(1-p)g_{m-1}.
\]
Induction shows that \(g_m\le 1/p\): substituting \(g_{m-1}\le1/p\) gives \(g_m\le1+(1-p)/p=1/p\). As the cap increases, these means approach the uncapped mean, so that mean \(g\) is finite. The same first-trial reasoning now gives
\[
g=1+(1-p)g,
\qquad g=\frac1p.
\]

If Awnik wins the first game, which happens with probability \(1/3\), he then waits for a loss. The expected additional wait is \(1/(2/3)=3/2\) games. If he loses first, with probability \(2/3\), the expected additional wait for a win is \(1/(1/3)=3\) games.

Including the first game and weighting these two cases by their probabilities, the expected total is
\[
1+\frac13\cdot\frac32+\frac23\cdot3
=1+\frac12+2
=\boxed{\frac72},
\]
choice \(\text{D}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Awnik is still playing after \(n\) games exactly when all \(n\) outcomes have been the same. This makes the probability of needing another game easy to calculate.

Let \(T\) be the total number of games played. For every integer \(n\ge1\), independence gives
\[
\Pr(T>n)=\left(\frac13\right)^n+\left(\frac23\right)^n.
\]
The two terms correspond to all wins and all losses, which are disjoint possibilities.

A total of \(k\) games contributes one unit for each of the \(k\) true statements \(T>0,T>1,\ldots,T>k-1\). Averaging this count gives
\[
\mathbb E[T]=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\Pr(T>n).
\]
Here \(\Pr(T>0)=1\). Both remaining sums are geometric series with ratios less than 1, so they converge, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[T]
&=1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac13\right)^n
  +\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac23\right)^n\\
&=1+\frac{1/3}{1-1/3}+\frac{2/3}{1-2/3}\\
&=1+\frac12+2
=\boxed{\frac72}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the answer is choice \(\text{D}\).
solutionMethods.label: Count the games still needed
